To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

low-dose ICF-I infusion in the depancreatized, hyperglycemic dog, under conditions of subbasal insulin administration, has no selective advantage in stimulating glucose utilization and suppressing glucose production and lipid mobilization over low-dose insulin.

low-dose IGH-I has no selective metabolic advantage over insulin in the regulation of glucose metabolism in hypergylcemic depancreatized dogs, i.e. in a model of type 1 diabetes, and that this is true for both conditions of declining and stable glucose concentrations.

(i), low-dose IGH-I has no selective metabolic advantage over insulin under conditions of hyper- or normoglycemia; (ii) the differential effects of low-dose infusions between IGF-I and low-dose insulin observed in the previous study during declining glucose levels are dose-related, but not due to differences between the two hormones.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of IGF-1 and insulin on glucose metabolism.
the effects of low-dose insulin-like growth factor-I (IGF-I) on glucose and lipid metabolism in the depancreatized (insulin-deficient) dog.
the role of IGF-I in glucose homeostasis.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
low-dose IGH-I has a metabolic profile similar to insulin, and is not a better therapeutic agent than insulin.
low-dose IGH-1 has no selective advantage in the treatment of hyperglycemic type 1 diabetes.
low-dose IGH-I is not superior to insulin in regulating glucose and lipid metabolism in hyperglycaemic, insulin-deficient depancreatized animals.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
IGF-I has little or no advantage over insulin in suppressing glucose and lipolysis or in stimulating glucose metabolism in insulin-deficient diabetes.
low-dose IGH-I is not superior to insulin in regulating glucose and lipid metabolism in insulin-deficient hyperglycemic dogs.
IGF-I and its analogues have no role as an adjunct to insulin in the treatment of insulin-deficient diabetes mellitus.
The main takeaway from our work is that
IGF-I has little advantage over insulin in the treatment of type 1 diabetes, at least at low doses.
low-dose IGC-I does not have any advantage over insulin in suppressing hepatic glucose production and stimulating glucose utilization during conditions of hyperglycaemia.
low dose IGF-I is no better than low dose insulin in suppressing glucose output, lipolysis and stimulating glucose uptake.
